# Postgres Gotchas

> Known PostgreSQL patterns that cause silent failures or hard-to-debug errors.

## Entries

- [CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS never retrofits constraints onto existing tables](create-table-if-not-exists-stale-constraints.md): Boot-applied schema.sql skips the whole CREATE statement on existing tables, so added FK ON DELETE CASCADE / SET NULL clauses never reach prod; code looks correct while the live constraint stays stale. HIGH.
- [ON CONFLICT must echo an expression-based unique index](on-conflict-expression-index.md): Upserting against a unique index on expressions (e.g. LEAST/GREATEST) requires repeating the exact expression in ON CONFLICT, not bare columns, or it errors 42P10. MEDIUM.
- [ORDER BY ... DESC defaults to NULLS FIRST, inverting a boolean preference clause](order-by-desc-nulls-first.md): A `ORDER BY (nullable_col = $1) DESC LIMIT 1` tie-break silently returns the opposite of its intent, because non-matching NULL rows evaluate to NULL (not false) and DESC sorts NULLS FIRST; add NULLS LAST. HIGH.
- [A column that exists but is NULL corpus-wide makes any filter on it silently match zero rows](filter-on-empty-column-matches-nothing.md): A column can be correctly typed and SELECTed by shipped code yet never written by the crawler/ETL, so `WHERE col <= $1` returns an empty set forever with no error and HTTP 200; profile with `count(col)` vs `count(*)` before building any predicate, and verify a deploy by diffing filtered vs unfiltered DATA rather than by status code. HIGH.
- [An empty cached column can be upstream-null, with the real signal in a sibling field the ETL drops](upstream-null-column-signal-in-dropped-sibling.md): On finding a NULL-corpus-wide column in an API-cached table, "the crawler is behind, re-crawl it" is often wrong -- the upstream may send null permanently while the real value arrives in a sibling field the upsert never gave a column, so the fix is a schema + ETL change rather than an ops rerun; profile the upstream payload and diff the ETL's insert column list against it, and beware that the deadest column is usually the best-named one for your use case. HIGH.
- [Retire the old live owner before transferring a partial-unique key](partial-unique-owner-transfer-order.md): An immediate partial unique index rejects a replacement owner if the old live row is retired later in the same transaction; soft-delete the old owner first. MEDIUM.
- [An empty API result makes a `NOT (col = ANY($1))` delete sweep wipe the whole table](empty-result-any-sweep-deletes-everything.md): The upsert-then-delete-what-was-not-returned reconciliation pattern is correct for every input except the empty array -- `ANY('{}')` matches nothing, so `NOT (...)` is TRUE for every row and the sweep deletes the tenant's entire mirror; an empty list arrives on a successful HTTP 200 from an outage, a revoked/downgraded credential, a renamed response key that a defensive `Array.isArray` guard turns into `[]`, or a pagination bug, and a snapshot job running after the sweep writes the loss into history where it cannot be backfilled. HIGH.
- [A negated comparison drops NULL rows into neither the set nor its complement](negated-comparison-drops-null-rows.md): `col <> 'x'` is not the opposite of `col = 'x'` -- a NULL col makes both evaluate to NULL, so the row is excluded from the filter *and* its inverse, and nothing errors; use IS DISTINCT FROM, spell out `(col IS NULL OR ...)` for NOT LIKE / NOT IN, and NOT EXISTS rather than a negated join, then assert `count(P) + count(NOT P) = count(*)` against real data. HIGH.
- [A forward-only migration runner skips a duplicate version forever](forward-only-runner-skips-duplicate-version.md): A runner selecting `version > MAX(version)` is correct only while migration numbers are unique, and concurrent agent sessions in one working tree routinely claim the same next number with no git conflict to warn them; if one duplicate lands and deploys first, every other file with that version is skipped on that deploy and every deploy after it, with no error, no pending entry, and a `schema_migrations` that reports up to date — select by ledger membership instead, and make the runner refuse a duplicate version outright. HIGH.
- [A nested BEGIN/COMMIT commits the outer transaction, so a "rolled back" verification writes to production](nested-begin-commit-ends-outer-transaction.md): Postgres has no nested transactions — a second `BEGIN` is ignored with only a WARNING and the next `COMMIT` commits everything, so the standard "open a transaction, run real code, roll back" harness silently writes to production the moment it calls a service function that manages its own transaction, and the closing `ROLLBACK` no-ops while the run reports success; translate inner BEGIN/COMMIT/ROLLBACK to savepoints, and assert the row count after the rollback rather than trusting it. HIGH.
- [The migration ledger's high-water mark is what decides, and it lies in both directions](ledger-high-water-mark-strands-migrations.md): a forward-only runner selects on production's applied mark, so `ls migrations/ | tail` before picking a number tests the wrong thing -- a concurrent session that commits a HIGHER number and deploys first strands yours with no collision at all, and a rollback that runs DROP TABLE without `DELETE FROM schema_migrations` leaves the mark pinned at a version nothing exists for, stranding every correct pending migration numbered BELOW it, written by other sessions who have no way to notice. Seen live with two ledger rows carrying real applied_at timestamps and not one of their fourteen tables present, silently burying a third package's migration. applied_at is not evidence; verify claims against pg_tables, query prod's mark immediately before committing, and select by ledger membership rather than `version > MAX(version)`. HIGH.
- [Rolling an aggregate up again with avg(avg) silently drops the sample weight](avg-of-avg-loses-sample-weight.md): Tiered rollups built from the tier below must weight by the sample count -- `avg(value_avg)` weighs a 3-sample bucket like a 300-sample one, and `min/max(value_avg)` takes extremes of averages so a spike vanishes at every zoom level; it is invisible in testing because steady-state buckets all carry equal counts, and diverges exactly at outage edges and the still-filling bucket. Measured: 300 samples at 10 plus 3 at 90 is 10.79 weighted and 50 naive. Carry sample_count on every rollup row, or the fix is unrecoverable once retention drops the raw points. HIGH.
- [A nullable column in a composite primary key silently disables ON CONFLICT deduplication](nullable-column-in-unique-key-breaks-dedup.md): NULL is never equal to NULL, so a key containing a nullable column never conflicts and every idempotent-retry INSERT appends instead; PRIMARY KEY implies NOT NULL and hides this, but the same key as a UNIQUE constraint or unique index -- which is what partitioning and partial indexes force you to -- does not, and it then fails for precisely the rows that omit the column, which are usually the most common ones. Use a NOT NULL DEFAULT '' sentinel and carry it out to the client contract. HIGH.
- [A CHECK constraint or VARCHAR width narrower than the type it stores fails only against a real database](check-constraint-narrower-than-its-type.md): An enum lives in the application type and in `VARCHAR(n) + CHECK (col IN (...))`, and the two drift with nothing to catch it -- tsc cannot see SQL, and a suite running against a fake DB has no column widths and no constraints, so every value passes. Two failures hide here: the CHECK omitting a value the type permits, and the column being too narrow for the longest value it permits, which Postgres rejects outright rather than truncating. Seen live as `product_type VARCHAR(16)` whose own CHECK listed the 17-character `domain_controller`, so every domain controller would have failed to store the one fact the column existed to record, while five unit tests asserting that distinction passed against a fake. The missing values are reliably the honest-failure states (`unknown`, `degraded`, `unavailable`), so a house rule to report `unknown` rather than `ok` gets silently reversed one layer below where it was written. Audit widths mechanically; prefer TEXT + CHECK; a CHECK wider than the type is safe, narrower is the bug. HIGH.
- [A stranded migration is not a pending migration, and applying it late can destroy live data](stranded-migration-is-not-pending.md): The two entries on how migrations get stranded stop at "renumbering is impossible after one applies"; this is what to do next, and the instinct is wrong. Giving a stranded file the next free version treats it as delayed-but-still-wanted, when its DDL was written against a schema that has since moved on -- and cleanup migrations, the `DROP TABLE ... CASCADE` kind, are both the likeliest to lose a version race and the only kind whose late application deletes data. Seen live: a file stranded in Aug 2025 drops nine tables, eight of which did go away on their own, while the ninth was re-adopted and now holds ~3,944 rows with 15 code references — renumbering it to tidy the ledger would have run a year-old DROP against live audit history. Two things hide it: only the objects UNIQUE to the file are missing (shared ones a later migration also declares are present, which reads as partial application but is not), and a schema dump taken where it did apply carries objects prod lacks, ours declaring an index on a column its own CREATE TABLE omits. Void it and tombstone the file, keeping the filename so the version stays claimed. HIGH.
- [A search predicate that matches a row does not make it findable](search-match-without-rank-is-unfindable.md): ORing an exact-key arm together with fuzzy FTS/ILIKE arms is correct on membership and silent on ordering -- the row IS in the result set but the caller's ORDER BY buries it past the LIMIT, so a search box returns unrelated rows and reads as "search cannot find record 234" while the WHERE clause, the one part that was right, absorbs the investigation. It scales inversely: short numeric terms are the most-typed and the worst case, since `ILIKE '%1%'` matches the corpus -- measured on one tenant, term `234` matched 93 rows with the exact match 4th, term `1` matched 4,078 with the exact match 378th and never on screen. Small fixtures hide it because everything fits one page. Carry the reason for the match into the ORDER BY (`(key = $n) DESC NULLS LAST` ahead of the caller's sort, reusing the bound param so no index shifts), let lookup-by-identifier opt out of the surface's default filters, and test RANK rather than membership -- count(*) passes on the broken query. HIGH.
